0 Wayfarers of the South Tigris Wayfarers of the South Tigris is set during the height of the Abbasid Caliphate, circa 820 AD. As brave explorers, cartographers and astronomers, players set off from Baghdad to map the surrounding land, waterways, and heavens above. Players must carefully manage their caravan of workers and equipment, while reporting back regularly to journal their findings at the House of Wisdom. Will you succeed in impressing the Caliph, or lose your way and succumb to the wilderness? [Rating: 1/10] Rules are so horribly worded that literally every player will be playing by different rules. It is so horribly worded that watching videos online about how to play literally contradict the rulebook. The rules books uses words like "only" and "cannot" while online video guides will tell you that you can and should do such action. They need to fix this rulebook, as it literally contradicts itself constantly.

[Rating: 1/10] A clever combination of dice placement, worker placement, and tableau engine building that winds up being fairly underwhelming once you get past the iconography soup to make competent decisions. The game has some serious issues with randomness in a way you'd least expect: there's a wealth of ways to mitigate the die rolls while having so few ways to mitigate the card market leading to players getting bottlenecked or trapped on the journal track, and player's gaining/never seeing the perfect combo pieces/scoring cards through pure luck of the draw. Wayfarers really could have been a much better

[Rating: 1/10] Every one of these games needs some weird mechanism to keep the hardcore euro fans occupied, and I guess here it's the bonus map.

[Rating: 1.8/10] Des mécaniques arbitraires de choix d'action pour des mécaniques arbitraires de résolution. Une narration complètement massacrée du coup.  Une iconographie bâclée. Une lisibilité inexistante. Des interactions subies mais pas vraiment choisies.  Plein de mécaniques artificiellement imbriquées.

[Rating: 2/10] Disgusting that a board game is set during a regime where minorities were oppressed under the rule one religion and yet the players seem to be playing as happy explorers traveling the land and charting the stars.

[Rating: 2/10] All you're doing is spinning wheels for 3 hours and then the game is over and you get to put it away.

[Rating: 2/10] Not a fan of this one and can't imagine an instance where I would play again. Not being able to refresh/wipe the cards is a serious flaw.  Resting seems more rewarding than using all your actions. I rarely used the actual workers and stuck with just the dice so I could push up the track faster. Speaking of the journal track, it is tedious and unforgiving if you make a wrong choice. It was so unenjoyable that I ended up trying to help another player push up the track just so the game could be over.

[Rating: 2/10] I did not enjoy this game at all. It is one of the prime examples of post-2010 eurogame design, where unnecessary mechanics and combinations there-of are added on top of each others in huge pile, so players have tons of options, but the gameplay is very difficult to grasp and learn. Additionally, the rulebook is just bad.

[Rating: 2/10] Terrible game IMO.  Mashed in concepts from Arnak, Raiders of the Lost Sea, and others.  Card font tiny and hard to read.  Color palette is low contrast so very hard to pick put small symbols against art background.  Could have made both larger with more contrast.  Symbol matching essential, but too many symbols.  Overall avoid.

[Rating: 2/10] There is just too much going on with this game. Too many options, too many chaining effects, too much AP making the time played very watered down. I really liked the ideas here with the tableau building, resting being rewarding, and the polyomino board.. but the execution is just not too my tastes. Im also just not a huge fan of the variety of scoring objective cards causing players to all be going there own direction for VP

[Rating: 2/10] I read the rules 3 times before getting it out to the table. I admired the thematic touches, and the different strategies, and was extremely hyped. Then after 30 minutes of playing it, I was already posting it for sale. I don't think I was ever this bored while playing a game, and I would only play this again  if I had a second life.

[Rating: 3/10] This one didn’t really land for me. I like the idea of the South Tigris series and the mix of exploration, dice placement, and engine building, but in practice it felt more fiddly than fun. There’s a lot going on, and I never quite felt like the systems came together in a satisfying way for me.  What keeps it from being something I’d want to revisit often is that the flow just feels a bit clunky. I can see what it’s going for, but it doesn’t give me that smooth, engaging decision-making loop I look for in heavier games. [Rating: 3/10] To weird and mathematical. No flow or sense of elegance. Feels like work, and not the good kind...

[Rating: 3/10] I love hefty games, but this one just doesn't play well, its complicated for the sake of being complicated, the rule book is mediocre and game play doesn't flow, engine building and scoring are too independent.

[Rating: 3/10] This is one of those games that has a ton of fiddly bits and left me asking, “Was it worth the effort?” And the answer for me was no. I will also note that I’m not a fan of games with very little player interaction. This is basically a solitaire game played in a group.
